::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
### Quick start

If someone has already set up TTpipe on your cluster and you just want a
run, these are the steps. Each one is explained in the sections below.

1. Clone the repository and `cd` into it ([Setup](#one-time-setup)).
2. Get a matching genome FASTA and GTF ([Reference](#the-reference)).
3. Download the FASTQ files ([Data](#the-data)).
4. Describe them in `samplesheet.txt` ([Samplesheet](#describe-your-samples)).
5. Point `config/TTpipeConfig.yaml` at your reference
   ([Config](#point-the-config-at-your-reference)).
6. Set `TTPIPE_PROFILE` and `TTPIPE_OUTPUT_ROOT` in `~/.bashrc`
   ([Compute site](#tell-ttpipe-which-cluster-you-are-on)).
7. Dry run: `bash TTpipe.sh -n` ([Dry run](#dry-run)).
8. Run: `sbatch TTpipe.sh`, then open `output/qc/TTpipe_qc_report.html`
   ([Run](#run-it), [QC](#read-the-qc-report)).
9. Look at the tables, tracks and figures ([Inspecting](#inspecting-the-outputs)).
:::

This page is a single walkthrough. The other chapters are reference pages;
this one takes you from an empty directory to a finished run and a look at
the results, in the order you would do things. **Every code block here is
illustrative and is not executed when the book is built: no output shown on
this page comes from a real run, and the paths and run accessions are
placeholders.** Read [Validation status](validation.qmd) for what has
actually been run.

## The example

The public dataset **GSE260914** (Magnitov et al. 2024) contains, among
other experiments, TT-seq of mouse embryonic stem cells in which the protein
ZFP143 is tagged with a degron (dTAG), so that adding the dTAG ligand makes
the cell destroy it. The TT-seq samples are:

| Condition | Meaning | Replicates |
|-----------|---------|------------|
| `DMSO` | Solvent only: the control (0 h of degradation) | 2 |
| `2H` | 2 hours after dTAG | 2 |
| `6H` | 6 hours after dTAG | 2 |
| `24H` | 24 hours after dTAG | 2 |

That is eight paired-end libraries. The question is: *which genes change
their transcription at each time point compared with DMSO?* You want the
tracks to look at, the per-gene table, the enrichment of gene sets, and a
check that the libraries are good.

## One-time setup

```bash
mkdir -p ~/ttseq_example && cd ~/ttseq_example
git clone https://github.com/jpflores-13/TTpipe.git
cd TTpipe
```

You need `python3` >= 3.11 and `conda` >= 24.7.1 on a **Linux** machine or
cluster ([Setup](setup.qmd); the tool versions TTpipe pins have no macOS
arm64 builds). You do not install STAR, samtools or R yourself: Snakemake
builds a conda environment for each group of rules the first time it needs
one.

## The reference

TTpipe needs a genome FASTA and a gene annotation (GTF) **from the same
source**, so that chromosome names match. Here: the GENCODE mouse release M25
annotation and the GENCODE GRCm38 primary assembly, which both call the
chromosomes `chr1`, `chr2`, ... (these URLs were checked to exist):

```bash
mkdir -p /path/to/reference && cd /path/to/reference
wget https://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/gencode/Gencode_mouse/release_M25/GRCm38.primary_assembly.genome.fa.gz
wget https://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/gencode/Gencode_mouse/release_M25/gencode.vM25.annotation.gtf.gz
gunzip GRCm38.primary_assembly.genome.fa.gz gencode.vM25.annotation.gtf.gz
```

Check the names match before going on:

```bash
grep '>' GRCm38.primary_assembly.genome.fa | head -3     # >chr1 ...
awk '$3=="gene"' gencode.vM25.annotation.gtf | head -2   # first column: chr1
```

::: {.callout-warning}
**The chromosome-name trap.** An Ensembl FASTA names chromosomes `1`, `2`,
`X`; a GENCODE GTF names them `chr1`, `chr2`, `chrX`. The source guide pairs
the two, and a pipeline that does so finds no genes (or fails when building
the STAR index). TTpipe does not check for this: you must. If you prefer UCSC
mm10, its per-chromosome files are at
<https://hgdownload.soe.ucsc.edu/goldenPath/mm10/chromosomes/>; concatenate
the ones you want into one FASTA and use it with the same GENCODE GTF.
:::

The STAR index is built once by TTpipe itself (next sections). It needs
roughly 32 GB of memory or more.

## The data

The reads are in the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA). **Do not copy run
accessions from a web page or another document; look them up.** The GEO page
for GSE260914 lists the samples; the ENA read-only API lists the runs. The
study also holds Hi-C, ChIP-seq and 4C experiments, so you must pick only the
TT-seq runs; their experiment titles start with `TTseq`:

```bash
curl -s 'https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/search?result=read_run&query=study_alias="GSE260914"&fields=run_accession,experiment_title,library_layout,fastq_ftp&format=tsv' \
    > ena_runs.tsv
grep TTseq ena_runs.tsv | cut -f1,2,3     # check: the titles, and that the layout is PAIRED
```

The eight TT-seq runs have titles of the form `TTseq_DMSO_rep1` or
`TTseq_dTAG_2H_rep1`. The listing has `fastq_ftp` as two paths separated by
`;` (read 1 and read 2). This loop downloads each run and renames it to the
sample names used in the samplesheet below (it is illustrative: check the
list printed by the `grep` above before running it):

```bash
mkdir -p /path/to/fastq && cd /path/to/fastq
grep TTseq /path/to/ena_runs.tsv | while IFS=$'\t' read -r run title layout ftp; do
    tag=$(echo "$title" | awk '{print $(NF-3)}')       # e.g. TTseq_dTAG_2H_rep1
    tag=${tag#TTseq_}; tag=${tag#dTAG_}                # e.g. 2H_rep1
    name="ZFP143_${tag}"
    r1=${ftp%%;*}; r2=${ftp##*;}
    wget -O "${name}_R1.fastq.gz" "ftp://${r1}"
    wget -O "${name}_R2.fastq.gz" "ftp://${r2}"
done
ls                                                     # eight pairs, e.g. ZFP143_2H_rep1_R1.fastq.gz
```

If your site blocks FTP, download the same files over HTTPS or with
`fasterq-dump` from the SRA Toolkit using the run accessions in the first
column of `ena_runs.tsv`.

## Describe your samples

`samplesheet.txt` is tab-separated, one row per sample (one pair of FASTQ
files). The shipped file already holds the eight samples:

```
Name              Condition  Replicate  Read1                          Read2                          Sequencing_Directory
ZFP143_DMSO_rep1  DMSO       rep1       ZFP143_DMSO_rep1_R1.fastq.gz   ZFP143_DMSO_rep1_R2.fastq.gz   /path/to/fastq/
ZFP143_DMSO_rep2  DMSO       rep2       ZFP143_DMSO_rep2_R1.fastq.gz   ZFP143_DMSO_rep2_R2.fastq.gz   /path/to/fastq/
ZFP143_2H_rep1    2H         rep1       ZFP143_2H_rep1_R1.fastq.gz     ZFP143_2H_rep1_R2.fastq.gz     /path/to/fastq/
...
ZFP143_24H_rep2   24H        rep2       ZFP143_24H_rep2_R1.fastq.gz    ZFP143_24H_rep2_R2.fastq.gz    /path/to/fastq/
```

Replace `/path/to/fastq/` with the folder you downloaded into. `Name` is
used in every file name; `Condition` groups the replicates; `Replicate` is
used by DESeq2 as a batch term. Use only letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`.

## Point the config at your reference

Open `config/TTpipeConfig.yaml`. For this example you change:

```yaml
samplesheet: 'samplesheet.txt'
genome_fasta: '/path/to/reference/GRCm38.primary_assembly.genome.fa'
gtf: '/path/to/reference/gencode.vM25.annotation.gtf'
star_index: '/path/to/reference/mm10_STARgenome'
build_star_index: true        # first run only
sjdb_overhang: 100            # read length - 1; check your read length
strandedness: 'dUTP'          # see the note below
reference_condition: 'DMSO'
condition_order: ['DMSO', '2H', '6H', '24H']
```

- **`strandedness`.** `dUTP` is the guide's assumption (read 1 antisense, read
  2 sense). TTpipe lets you state it, and the QC report's strandedness panel
  checks it afterwards. If that panel shows most reads on the wrong strand,
  see [Recipes](recipes.qmd#strandedness-dutp-or-forward).
- **`sjdb_overhang`.** Read length minus one; 100 matches 101-base reads. Check
  the read length in your FastQC report; the setting only matters when the
  index is built.
- **`build_star_index: true`** builds the index into `star_index` as part of
  this run. After the first successful run set it back to `false` so that the
  index is reused.
- **`condition_order`** only sets the order in plots and the Sankey diagram.

For gene-set enrichment, download gene sets yourself (for example mouse
collections from MSigDB, as `.gmt` files with gene symbols) and list them:

```yaml
gsea_collections:
  Hallmarks: '/path/to/mh.all.v2023.2.Mm.symbols.gmt'
  GO_BP: '/path/to/m5.go.bp.v2023.2.Mm.symbols.gmt'
```

(The file names are examples; use the version you download.) Leave
`gsea_collections: {}` to skip GSEA. Every other key keeps the guide's
default; [Configuration](configuration.qmd) explains all of them.

## Tell TTpipe which cluster you are on

Put these in `~/.bashrc` once (see [Cluster reference](cluster.qmd)):

```bash
export TTPIPE_PROFILE=profiles/<your-site>          # e.g. profiles/biowulf
export TTPIPE_OUTPUT_ROOT=/path/to/scratch/ttpipe   # where `output/` goes
export TTPIPE_EMAIL=you@university.edu              # optional: start / finish / failure emails
source ~/.bashrc
```

If your cluster is not one of the shipped profiles, copy
`profiles/slurm-template` and fill in your account and partition. On one
machine with no scheduler the default `profiles/local` is used. The
per-rule memory and time in the profiles are starting guesses; expect to
adjust them after a first look at what the jobs used.

## Dry run

```bash
bash TTpipe.sh -n
```

This prints every job Snakemake would run, and a table that counts them by
rule, and starts nothing. For this example you should see, for instance,
eight `star_align` jobs (one per sample) and sixteen `fastqc` jobs (two
mates per sample). If it stops with an error about the samplesheet or a
config key, fix that first; the messages name the problem.

## Run it

```bash
sbatch TTpipe.sh            # on a SLURM cluster
# bash TTpipe.sh            # on one machine (profiles/local)
```

The launcher job is small; it submits each rule as its own job. The first run
also builds the conda environments, which takes a while and needs memory, so
the launcher asks for 16 GB. Watch progress with `squeue -u $USER`, the
launcher's `TTpipe-<jobid>.out`, and the logs under
`<outputDir>/<sample>/logs/` and `<outputDir>/logs/`. If a run stops, release
the lock and resubmit; finished steps are kept:

```bash
bash unlock.sh
sbatch TTpipe.sh
```

## Read the QC report

Open `output/qc/TTpipe_qc_report.html` in a browser. Go through it in this
order ([Reading the QC report](qc.qmd) explains each part):

1. **Skipped or partial sections**: anything that could not be drawn, and why.
2. **Per-sample QC table**: one row per sample, with a traffic light per
   metric. Look for any sample that stands out from its replicate.
3. **Strandedness**: the share of reads on the gene's strand. If it is low for
   every sample, `strandedness` is set to the wrong library type.
4. **Alignment, duplication, rRNA**: as in any RNA-seq QC.
5. **Correlation and PCA**: replicates should sit together; conditions
   should separate in the direction you expect from the time course.

`output/qc/TTpipe_multiqc.html` is a standard MultiQC page for FastQC, STAR
and Picard; use it if you are used to that layout.

## Inspecting the outputs

The layout of `output/` (see the [README](https://github.com/jpflores-13/TTpipe#output-structure)
for the full tree):

```
output/
├── qc/                TTpipe_qc_report.html  TTpipe_multiqc.html  sample_qc.tsv
├── ZFP143_DMSO_rep1/  ZFP143_DMSO_rep1.bam  _forward.bam  _reverse.bam  stats/  counts/  logs/
├── merged/            DMSO.bam  DMSO_forward.bam  ...
├── tracks/            DMSO.bw  DMSO_forward.bw  DMSO_reverse.bw  ...  scale_factors.tsv
├── counts/            counts_deseq2.txt  counts_forward.txt  counts_reverse.txt  gene_info.tsv
└── analysis/          deseq2/  gsea/  figures/
```

**Tracks.** Load `tracks/*.bw` into a genome browser (for example IGV, with
the mm10 genome whose chromosome names are `chr1`...). `DMSO_forward.bw` is
signal from RNA transcribed from the + strand and `DMSO_reverse.bw` from the -
strand. `tracks/scale_factors.tsv` lists the scale factor applied to each
condition.

**Differential expression.** One table per comparison:
`analysis/deseq2/degs_2H_vs_DMSO.csv`, `..._6H_vs_DMSO.csv`,
`..._24H_vs_DMSO.csv`. Read one in R and list the genes below the 0.01
adjusted p-value cut-off:

```r
d <- read.csv("output/analysis/deseq2/degs_6H_vs_DMSO.csv")
info <- read.delim("output/counts/gene_info.tsv")
d <- merge(d, info[, c("gene_id", "gene_name")], by = "gene_id")
sig <- subset(d, !is.na(padj) & padj < 0.01)
head(sig[order(sig$padj), c("gene_name", "log2FoldChange", "padj")])
```

A positive `log2FoldChange` means more new RNA 6 hours after dTAG than in
DMSO. `analysis/deseq2/deg_summary.tsv` has the numbers of up and down genes
per comparison, and `analysis/figures/pca.pdf` is the PCA of the VST
counts.

**Gene sets.** If you gave `gsea_collections`, there is one table per
collection and comparison, for example `analysis/gsea/Hallmarks_6H_vs_DMSO.tsv`:

```r
g <- read.delim("output/analysis/gsea/Hallmarks_6H_vs_DMSO.tsv")
head(g[order(g$padj), c("pathway", "NES", "padj")])
```

A positive `NES` means the set sits toward the top of the ranked list (more
transcription in 6 h than DMSO).

**The Sankey diagram.** `analysis/figures/sankey.pdf` shows, for genes tested in
all three comparisons, how many are up, down or unchanged at 2 h, 6 h and 24 h
and how genes flow between categories. The underlying table is
`analysis/deseq2/sankey_categories.tsv`.

[Differential expression and GSEA](analysis.qmd) explains these files column by
column.
